title: Before you sacrifice, count every piece that must arrive
outcomes: Writes out a forcing line and lists the pieces that must move or support
Sees that a quiet piece, such as a bishop behind a rook, can be the one that decides
Declines to start when one needed piece cannot arrive
Ignores changes on the other wing

steps.text: A direct attack is a commitment. After the first sacrifice you cannot take it back, and his replies are mostly forced. So **before** the first move, write the whole line, list every piece that must move or support, and check that each can arrive. The last piece to arrive often decides (a **rule of thumb**). If one piece cannot come, do not start yet.

steps.caption: White to move. Count the pieces the line needs.

line.say: The rook takes h6 with check. In the engine's line Black takes it.
The queen takes h6 with check. The rook has left g6, so the bishop on d3 now looks at h7.
Qxh7 is checkmate. The bishop protects the queen.

claims.statement: Rxh6+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
At the end two white pieces attack h7: the queen and the bishop.
Only the black king defends h7 at that moment.

steps.text: Count the quiet pieces too. Here the bishop does nothing until the rook leaves g6, yet without it the mate fails. A simple winning move, if you have one, is often better than a long attack you cannot see to the end: a **rule of thumb** that these positions do not test. This lesson does not cover when to break off an attack or repeat moves.

steps.title: One position, three small changes
steps.prompt: Predict for each: does Rxh6+ work? Then check.

Before the next sacrifice in one of your games, write the line and list the pieces it needs on a piece of paper. Afterwards, note whether every piece could arrive. Today: which piece would you most likely have left out of the list?
